questions.q: What is the main purpose of secondary storage in a DBMS?
options: To permanently store large amounts of data
To execute SQL statements
To replace the query optimizer
To hold only CPU instructions
questions.explanation: Secondary storage such as SSDs and hard disks provides non-volatile, long-term storage for database files.

questions.q: Which storage device generally has no moving mechanical parts?
options: Magnetic tape
Hard disk drive
Solid-state drive
Optical disc
questions.explanation: An SSD stores data in flash memory and has no spinning platters or moving read/write head.

questions.q: What is a database block (page)?
options: A SQL command
A fixed-size unit of data transferred between storage and memory
A database user account
A type of index key
questions.explanation: A DBMS commonly transfers data between disk and main memory in page-sized units.

questions.q: Why does a DBMS use a buffer manager?
options: To translate SQL into relational algebra
To create user passwords
To compress every query
To manage database pages cached in main memory
questions.explanation: The buffer manager controls which disk pages are kept in memory and handles page reads and writes.

questions.q: What is a buffer hit?
options: The requested page is already present in the buffer pool
The requested page is corrupted
A transaction has been aborted
An index has no root node
questions.explanation: A buffer hit occurs when the required page is found in memory, avoiding a disk read.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a dirty page flag?
options: It marks a page as encrypted
It indicates that the page has been modified in memory and must eventually be written
It identifies an empty table
It marks a transaction as read-only
questions.explanation: A dirty page contains changes not yet written to the persistent database file.

questions.q: Which replacement policy removes the page that has not been used for the longest time?
options: FIFO
MRU
LRU
Random
questions.explanation: Least Recently Used (LRU) selects the page whose most recent access is farthest in the past.

questions.q: In a database file, what is a record?
options: A collection of related fields describing one row
A complete database server
A query execution plan
A storage device
questions.explanation: A record stores the field values belonging to one tuple or row.

questions.q: Which file organization stores records in no particular order based on a search key?
options: Sequential sorted organization
Clustered organization
Hashed organization
Heap file organization
questions.explanation: A heap file stores records without maintaining an order on a particular search attribute.

questions.q: What is a major advantage of a sequential sorted file?
options: It never requires disk space
It supports efficient sequential and range access on the ordering key
It prevents duplicate values automatically
It makes every update constant-time
questions.explanation: Sorted records can be read in key order and ranges can be located efficiently.

questions.q: What is an index in a DBMS?
options: A copy of the entire application
A transaction log
An auxiliary structure that helps locate records
A constraint that forbids NULL
questions.explanation: An index stores search-key values with references that help the DBMS find corresponding records.

questions.q: What does a search key in an index represent?
options: One or more attributes used to locate records
The password used by a database user
The physical size of a disk
The name of a database view
questions.explanation: The search key is the attribute or attribute set on which the index is built.

questions.q: A primary index is commonly built on which attribute?
options: An attribute that is never queried
A non-key attribute with duplicates
A temporary variable
The ordering key of a file that is physically ordered on that key
questions.explanation: A primary index is associated with a data file ordered on its primary ordering key.

questions.q: What is a clustering index?
options: An index on a random expression only
An index on an ordering non-key attribute whose values may repeat
An index that stores only NULL values
An index used only for passwords
questions.explanation: A clustering index supports a file ordered by a non-key attribute, so several records may share a value.

questions.q: What is a secondary index?
options: An index that determines the physical ordering of the data file
A database backup
An additional index whose search order differs from the file's physical ordering
A transaction schedule
questions.explanation: A secondary index provides another access path and does not define the file's physical order.

questions.q: What is a dense index?
options: An index with an entry for every search-key value or every record, depending on the index design
An index with no entries
An index containing only the first record
An index that stores SQL text
questions.explanation: A dense index has an index entry for each search-key value or record, enabling direct lookup through the index.

questions.q: What is a sparse index?
options: An index containing every possible key
An index stored only in RAM
An index with no pointer fields
An index containing entries for only some search-key values, often one per data block
questions.explanation: A sparse index uses fewer entries and generally relies on the data file being ordered.

questions.q: Which condition usually allows a sparse index to work correctly?
options: The file must be encrypted
The data file must be ordered on the index search key
Every row must have a NULL key
The table must contain one row
questions.explanation: Ordering lets the DBMS find the relevant block from a smaller set of index entries.

questions.q: What is a multilevel index?
options: An index that supports multiple users only
An index containing several unrelated tables
An index built over another index to reduce search levels
A list of all SQL keywords
questions.explanation: When an index is too large, another index level can be built over it to speed up searching.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a B-tree?
options: To support balanced search, insertion and deletion
To store only text documents
To remove all duplicate rows
To replace transaction logging
questions.explanation: A B-tree is a balanced search tree designed to support efficient dynamic indexing.

questions.q: What does it mean for a B-tree to be height-balanced?
options: Every node has exactly one key
All leaves are at the same depth
The root is always a leaf
Every internal node has two children
questions.explanation: In a B-tree, all leaf nodes occur at the same level, keeping the tree balanced.

questions.q: In a B-tree, where can search-key values be stored?
options: Only in the root
Only in leaf nodes
Only outside the tree
In both internal and leaf nodes
questions.explanation: A B-tree can store keys and record pointers in internal as well as leaf nodes.

questions.q: What is a key difference between a B-tree and a B+ tree?
options: B+ trees do not have a root
B-trees cannot be searched
B+ trees store data entries at leaves and use internal nodes mainly for navigation
B+ trees cannot contain duplicate search keys
questions.explanation: In a B+ tree, data entries or record pointers are stored at leaf level; internal nodes guide searches.

questions.q: Why are B+ tree leaf nodes often linked?
options: To support efficient sequential and range scans
To encrypt the index
To prevent insertion
To store transaction passwords
questions.explanation: Linked leaves let the DBMS move through adjacent key values without repeatedly returning to the root.

questions.q: What happens when a B+ tree leaf node overflows during insertion?
options: The whole database is deleted
The node is split and a separator key may be propagated upward
The root is always removed
All keys are converted to strings
questions.explanation: A split creates space while preserving order and balance; a separator is inserted into the parent.

questions.q: What is the root node's role in a tree index?
options: It stores only deleted rows
It is always the final data page
It is the starting point for traversing the index
It contains the transaction log
questions.explanation: A search begins at the root and follows child pointers toward the target key.

questions.q: What is the order or fan-out of a tree index related to?
options: The number of database users
The number of SQL statements in a file
The number of columns in every table
The maximum number of child pointers a node can contain
questions.explanation: Fan-out describes how many child pointers an internal node can have and strongly affects tree height.

questions.q: Why are B+ trees suitable for range queries?
options: Their leaves are ordered and commonly linked
They store no keys
They require scanning every database table
They support equality searches only
questions.explanation: Ordered linked leaves make it efficient to continue from the first matching key through the requested range.

questions.q: What is hashing in database file organization?
options: Sorting records alphabetically
Using a hash function to map a search key to a bucket
Encrypting each database page
Combining two relations
questions.explanation: A hash function computes a bucket address from a search-key value.

questions.q: What is a bucket in a hash file?
options: A SQL constraint
A query plan
A storage location that can hold one or more records
A B-tree root
questions.explanation: A bucket is the unit or page area to which records are assigned by the hash function.

questions.q: What is a hash collision?
options: Two different keys map to the same bucket
A transaction reads its own update
A table has no primary key
A query returns no rows
questions.explanation: A collision occurs when distinct search-key values produce the same hash address.

questions.q: What is overflow chaining in hashing?
options: Moving every record into a B+ tree
Deleting colliding records
Sorting the buckets by date
Linking additional overflow buckets when the target bucket is full
questions.explanation: Overflow chaining provides extra storage for records that cannot fit in their home bucket.

questions.q: Which query type is hashing particularly effective for?
options: A broad range search such as BETWEEN
An equality search on the hashed key
Sorting all rows by the key
Finding the minimum key in order
questions.explanation: Hashing is designed for equality lookups; it does not naturally preserve key order for range scans.

questions.q: Why is a basic hash index generally unsuitable for range queries?
options: It stores every key twice
It requires a sorted file
Hashing does not preserve the ordering of search-key values
It cannot store numeric keys
questions.explanation: Nearby key values may map to unrelated buckets, so a range cannot be scanned in key order.

questions.q: What is static hashing?
options: A scheme with a fixed number of primary buckets
A scheme that changes the hash function for every query
A tree with linked leaves
A method that stores no bucket addresses
questions.explanation: Static hashing begins with a fixed bucket structure; growth may lead to overflow chains or reorganization.

questions.q: What is dynamic hashing designed to handle?
options: Only read-only databases
Tables with exactly one row
Queries without conditions
Growth and shrinkage of the data set by adapting the bucket structure
questions.explanation: Dynamic hashing expands or contracts its directory or bucket organization as the file changes.

questions.q: In extendible hashing, what does the directory contain?
options: Only the actual record values
Pointers to buckets indexed by hash prefixes
SQL statements for updates
The list of database users
questions.explanation: The directory uses a number of hash bits to point to the appropriate bucket.

questions.q: What is the global depth in extendible hashing?
options: The number of records in the largest bucket
The number of database tables
The number of hash bits used to index the directory
The number of transactions in a schedule
questions.explanation: Global depth determines the directory size, which is typically 2 raised to the global depth.

questions.q: What is local depth in extendible hashing?
options: The number of hash bits that distinguish a particular bucket
The number of columns in a table
The number of pages in the buffer pool
The number of levels in a B-tree
questions.explanation: Local depth records how many hash-prefix bits are significant for a particular bucket.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a composite index?
options: To index only NULL values
To index multiple tables without a join
To store multiple database backups
To use more than one column as the index search key
questions.explanation: A composite index is built on an ordered combination of two or more columns.

questions.q: Why can an index speed up a query but slow down data modification?
options: Indexes eliminate all disk I/O
Insertions, deletions and updates may also require index maintenance
Indexes make tables smaller in every case
Indexes prevent transaction conflicts
questions.explanation: The DBMS must keep index entries consistent whenever indexed data changes.

questions.q: What is a covering index for a query?
options: An index that contains all columns needed by that query
An index that stores the whole database backup
An index that can only be used once
An index with no search key
questions.explanation: A covering index can satisfy the query using index data without fetching the base table rows.

questions.q: What is the selectivity of a search condition?
options: The number of indexes in a database
The number of pages in a disk
The fraction of rows expected to satisfy the condition
The number of transactions waiting for locks
questions.explanation: A selective condition matches a small fraction of rows and may make an index access path attractive.

questions.q: Which index is often useful for a column with many repeated values?
options: An index that is never maintained
A bitmap index in workloads suited to bitmap operations
A hash index for ordered range scans
A unique index that forbids duplicates
questions.explanation: Bitmap indexes can be effective for low-cardinality columns in suitable analytical workloads.

questions.q: What does a unique index enforce?
options: Every indexed key value is distinct
All rows have identical values
The table is physically sorted
The index has exactly one page
questions.explanation: A unique index prevents two rows from having the same indexed key combination, subject to DBMS NULL rules.

questions.q: What is index selectivity generally higher for?
options: A gender-like column with few values
A Boolean flag
A column with one repeated value
A column with many distinct values relative to its row count
questions.explanation: A column with many distinct values tends to have higher selectivity for equality predicates.

questions.q: What is a full table scan?
options: Reading only the root of an index
Reading all data pages of a table to examine its rows
Reading only the transaction log
Searching one hash bucket
questions.explanation: A full table scan examines the table's data pages, which can be efficient when many rows are needed.

questions.q: When might a DBMS prefer a table scan over an index lookup?
options: When the query needs a large fraction of the table
When the table has no rows
Whenever an index exists
Only when the query contains ORDER BY
questions.explanation: If many rows are required, repeated index lookups can cost more than reading the table sequentially.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off when creating many indexes?
options: More indexes always reduce storage use
More indexes remove the need for backups
Read performance may improve, but storage and update costs increase
Indexes guarantee serializable schedules
questions.explanation: Indexes consume disk space and must be maintained during data modifications.

questions.q: Which structure is commonly preferred for equality lookup when key order is unnecessary?
options: A linked list
A hash index
A sequential scan of unrelated tables
A transaction wait-for graph
questions.explanation: Hash indexes are designed for fast equality lookup, though they do not support ordered range traversal well.
